grade_rationale: Correct product (ethanol + bromide), single balanced concerted step, backside attack with correct curved arrows.
Right product and right mechanism, but the nucleophile arrow points at the methyl carbon (atom:0) instead of the electrophilic CH2 (atom:1): one electron-pushing error.
Final product is dimethyl ether (a constitutional isomer of ethanol) — impossible by SN2 on bromoethane; wrong connectivity even though it is mass/charge balanced.
Product keeps both OH and Br on the same carbon giving a pentavalent carbon — not a real molecule.
Correct product drawn (ethanol + bromide) but the hydroxide nucleophile is omitted from the reactant side, so oxygen/hydrogen/charge are not conserved.
Textbook SN1 solvolysis of tert-butyl bromide: ionization to the tertiary carbocation, water capture, deprotonation to tert-butanol; every step balanced.
Correct intermediates and product, but in step 2 the water lone-pair arrow attacks a methyl carbon (atom:0) instead of the cationic center (atom:1): one arrow wrong.

Ionizes to a primary (isobutyl) carbocation instead of the tertiary one — the wrong, far-less-stable intermediate — and consequently reaches isobutanol; steps balance but the mechanism is conceptually wrong.
Correct ionization and water capture, but the final step lets bromide recombine, so the drawn final product is the starting tert-butyl bromide rather than tert-butanol.
Reaches tert-butanol, but the final deprotonation omits the water base and the released proton, so the last step does not conserve mass/charge.

Legitimate two-step variant: after ionization, water adds and a second water removes the proton in one concerted step to give tert-butanol + hydronium; balanced and correct, just fewer discrete steps than the reference.
Concerted E2 of 2-bromopropane by hydroxide: anti-periplanar removal of a beta-H, C=C formation, loss of bromide, giving propene + water + bromide; balanced with the three standard arrows.
Correct propene product, but the C-Br arrow is drawn from bromide back into the C-Br bond (reversed electron flow): one arrow wrong.
Draws cyclopropane (a 1,3 ring closure) instead of propene. Cyclopropane is a constitutional isomer of propene so it balances, but it is the wrong product for base-promoted elimination.
Correct propene product, but the hydroxide base is omitted and the abstracted proton simply disappears, so hydrogen and charge are not conserved.
E1 of tert-butyl bromide: ionization to the tertiary carbocation, then water removes a beta-H to give isobutylene + hydronium; balanced with correct arrows.
Correct carbocation and isobutylene product, but in step 2 the base arrow points at the cationic carbon (atom:1) as if adding, rather than abstracting the beta-H (atom:0): one arrow wrong.
Correct tertiary carbocation, but the drawn alkene is 1-butene, which requires a linear carbon skeleton impossible from the tert-butyl cation; wrong product.
Reaches isobutylene by having bromide (rather than solvent water) act as the base that removes the beta-H, giving isobutylene + HBr; any available base is acceptable, so this is a valid alternative.
Electrophilic aromatic bromination: benzene pi system attacks Br+ to give the arenium (Wheland) intermediate, then a base removes the ipso proton to rearomatize to bromobenzene; balanced.
Correct arenium and bromobenzene, but the first arrow is drawn from Br+ into the ring rather than from the aromatic pi bond to Br+ (reversed electron flow): one arrow wrong.
Draws the arenium with the positive charge on the ipso carbon that bears the bromine — a non-contributing resonance form; the real sigma complex delocalizes the charge ortho/para to the sp3 center.
Puts two bromines on a single aromatic ring carbon, giving a four-coordinate aromatic carbon — not a valid structure.
Cyanohydrin formation from acetaldehyde: cyanide adds to the carbonyl carbon to give an alkoxide, which is then protonated to the cyanohydrin; both steps balanced with correct arrows.
Correct alkoxide and cyanohydrin, but the nucleophile arrow attacks the carbonyl oxygen (atom:2) instead of the carbonyl carbon (atom:1): one arrow wrong.
Correct alkoxide, but the final product is drawn as ethyl cyanate (C-O-CN) — a constitutional isomer of the cyanohydrin with the wrong connectivity; wrong product.
Reaches the correct cyanohydrin, but the protonation step omits the proton source, so the added hydrogen and the charge are not conserved.
Reaches the cyanohydrin by protonating the alkoxide with water (giving hydroxide) instead of HCN; solvent protonation is a valid alternative proton source.
